g.text: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has proven to be successful in
improving reasoning capabilities of LLMs by optimizing against
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=0) Reinforcement Learning (RL) has proven to be successful in improving reasoning capabilities of LLMs by optimizing against task-specific reward signals.

g.text: Early successes in this direction include RL from Human Feedback
(RLHF) for aligning LLMs with human intent, most notably in
InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022) and ChatGPT (Achiam et al.,
g.title: N2 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) Early successes in this direction include RL from Human Feedback (RLHF) for aligning LLMs with human intent, most notably in InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022) and ChatGPT (Achiam et al., 2023), which have demonstrated that incorporating preference-based rewards can dramatically improve both the usability and correctness of model outputs.

g.text: Recently DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025) proposed a distinguishing feature
which is the so-called zero configuration, wherein the RL process directly
g.title: N3 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) Recently DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025) proposed a distinguishing feature which is the so-called zero configuration, wherein the RL process directly enhances the base language model.

g.text: This breakthrough started several efforts which were targeted at replicating
DeepSeek-R1’s methodology or refining its underlying RL mechanisms (Zeng et
al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2025; Hu et al.,
g.title: N4 [Prior_Work] (cites=5) This breakthrough started several efforts which were targeted at replicating DeepSeek-R1’s methodology or refining its underlying RL mechanisms (Zeng et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025).

g.text: Yet, in the realm of complex reasoning, RL algorithms typically do
not incorporate any form of feedback or reflection on the model’s
g.title: N5 [Limitation] (cites=0) Yet, in the realm of complex reasoning, RL algorithms typically do not incorporate any form of feedback or reflection on the model’s own outputs.

g.text: Humans, by contrast, rarely solve nontrivial problems in a single
pass: they often iterate on initial drafts, identify mistakes, and
refine their solutions based on internal feedback (Flower & Hayes,
g.title: N6 [Context] (cites=6) Humans, by contrast, rarely solve nontrivial problems in a single pass: they often iterate on initial drafts, identify mistakes, and refine their solutions based on internal feedback (Flower & Hayes, 1981; Simon, 2012; Braidotti, 2019; Flavell, 1979; Schön, 2017; Polya, 2014).

g.text: There is growing evidence that self-feedback mechanisms can
bolster multi-step reasoning and the capacity to correct errors
g.title: N7 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) There is growing evidence that self-feedback mechanisms can bolster multi-step reasoning and the capacity to correct errors (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023).

g.text: However, existing RL frameworks do not capitalize on this
iterative refinement process, leaving a critical gap between how
humans naturally solve problems and how LLMs are typically trained
g.title: N8 [Limitation] (cites=0) However, existing RL frameworks do not capitalize on this iterative refinement process, leaving a critical gap between how humans naturally solve problems and how LLMs are typically trained to do so.

g.text: In this work, we propose to fill this gap with Iterative GRPO (iGRPO) which
is a powerful extension of GRPO (Shao et al., 2024).
g.title: N9 [Method] (cites=1) In this work, we propose to fill this gap with Iterative GRPO (iGRPO) which is a powerful extension of GRPO (Shao et al., 2024).

g.text: As illustrated in Figure 1, Our method operates in two stages.
g.title: N10 [Method] (cites=0) As illustrated in Figure 1, Our method operates in two stages.

g.text: First, we draw multiple candidate completions from the model and compute
their relative rewards via the group-based mechanism of GRPO.
g.title: N11 [Method: stage-1] (cites=0) First, we draw multiple candidate completions from the model and compute their relative rewards via the group-based mechanism of GRPO.

g.text: We then select the highest-scoring draft and this serves as the
g.title: N12 [Method: stage-1] (cites=0) We then select the highest-scoring draft and this serves as the "first-draft" output of the model.

g.text: We consider this highest-scoring response as a guide to improve the final
g.title: N13 [Method: stage-2] (cites=0) We consider this highest-scoring response as a guide to improve the final output.

g.text: Hence, it is provided as a self-feedback to the model.
g.title: N14 [Method: stage-2] (cites=0) Hence, it is provided as a self-feedback to the model.

g.text: feed draft + prompt back to model
We feed it back to the model alongside the original prompt.
g.title: N15 [Method: stage-2] (cites=0) We feed it back to the model alongside the original prompt.

g.text: By conditioning on this exemplar, the second stage encourages the model to
refine and surpass its own best prior attempt.
g.title: N16 [Method: stage-2] (cites=0) By conditioning on this exemplar, the second stage encourages the model to refine and surpass its own best prior attempt.

g.text: Notably, this design preserves the efficiency of GRPO while introducing only
minimal extra overhead, as iGRPO still relies on the same set of group-based
g.title: N17 [Method] (cites=0) Notably, this design preserves the efficiency of GRPO while introducing only minimal extra overhead, as iGRPO still relies on the same set of group-based reward signals.

g.text: In doing so, iGRPO offers a promising avenue for self-guided
improvement, enabling LLMs to iteratively improve their reasoning
g.title: N18 [Contribution] (cites=0) In doing so, iGRPO offers a promising avenue for self-guided improvement, enabling LLMs to iteratively improve their reasoning capabilities.

g.text: We conduct a series of controlled experiments to compare iGRPO and GRPO
under identical training conditions, using different base models trained on
the Mathematics Aptitude Test of Heuristics (MATH) (Hendrycks et al., 2021)
g.title: N19 [Method] (cites=1) We conduct a series of controlled experiments to compare iGRPO and GRPO under identical training conditions, using different base models trained on the Mathematics Aptitude Test of Heuristics (MATH) (Hendrycks et al., 2021) dataset.

g.text: Specifically, we evaluate DeepSeek-R1 Distilled (Guo et al., 2025) and
OpenMath-Nemotron (Moshkov et al., 2025) on an extensive array of
mathematical reasoning benchmarks, including AIME24 (AI-MO, 2024a), AIME25
g.title: N20 [Method] (cites=8) Specifically, we evaluate DeepSeek-R1 Distilled (Guo et al., 2025) and OpenMath-Nemotron (Moshkov et al., 2025) on an extensive array of mathematical reasoning benchmarks, including AIME24 (AI-MO, 2024a), AIME25 (OpenCompass, 2025), MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2023), AMC23 (AI-MO, 2024b), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), and Minerva Math (Lewkowycz et al., 2022).

g.text: For models with 7B and 14B parameters, iGRPO consistently outperforms
g.title: N21 [Result] (cites=0) For models with 7B and 14B parameters, iGRPO consistently outperforms standard GRPO.

g.text: Moreover, by leveraging iGRPO algorithm with OpenReasoning-Nemotron-7B model
(NVIDIA, 2025) on the large-scale AceReason-Math (Chen et al., 2025b)
dataset (R1, 2024), we push the state of the art on AIME24 and AIME25 to
g.title: N22 [Result] (cites=3) Moreover, by leveraging iGRPO algorithm with OpenReasoning-Nemotron-7B model (NVIDIA, 2025) on the large-scale AceReason-Math (Chen et al., 2025b) dataset (R1, 2024), we push the state of the art on AIME24 and AIME25 to 85.62% and 79.64%, respectively.

g.text: self-feedback effective for RL math reasoning
These findings underscore the effectiveness of incorporating a
self-feedback stage into group-based RL optimization, particularly
g.title: N23 [Contribution] (cites=0) These findings underscore the effectiveness of incorporating a self-feedback stage into group-based RL optimization, particularly for complex mathematical reasoning tasks.
